utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, and as everyone would be aware we started off this week with one of those reminders that in this modern world we're all enslaved to the vagaries of technology. And you would have observed the priesthood of that craft coming with their incantations and rituals, and I gather that the problems have been corrected, so the usher has informed me. One of the unfortunate effects of this is that we would have lost about 35 to 40 minutes which we -- which we could not immediately make up because bearing in mind that the accused men would have been in court to begin on time as the schedule would have set out, that we should take the usual breaks in order that the rhythm and system in place for their convenience and comfort is not disrupted. On Thursday, before the -- we took the adjournment, the Chamber heard directly from the accused about their -- certain difficulties that they were experiencing in terms of their -- the arrangements made for them, particularly in light of the extended sittings that have been arranged for this week. Among the complaints which they would have raised would have been certain questions related to security, and I would repeat what we would have said on Thursday, that the Chamber would say nothing directly in response to those complaints because for obvious reasons the Chamber would defer to the security team and the systems they have in place. And if there is a problem over and beyond the ordinary incidents attendant to being in custody, the accused persons through their counsel would, no doubt, formulate the appropriate applications. And unless and until that arises, we say nothing further about that. A matter of concern to us is the consequence of the extended sittings for this week, in that the routine, as we are advised, that is in place for the accused to take their fresh-air exercise in the late afternoon could not be met because of the impossibility of meshing the transport arrangements from the Tribunal -- from the seat of the Tribunal back to the Detention Centre. And the three days, possibly four, which would occur this week, the only assurance that we're able to give is that the provisions within the detention facilities for exercise, albeit not in the fresh air, would somehow compensate for that inconvenience which we recognise our decision to have extended sittings would have occasioned. So we trust that the accused, particularly Mr. Zupljanin who would have articulated the concerns on behalf -- more so than his co-accused, that he understands what we said. We recognise that our explanation isn't satisfactory, but that is the -- as much as we're able to say at this point. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, Matthew Olmsted, Joanna Korner, and case manager Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Slobodan Cvijetic appearing for Stanisic Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. This morning for Zupljanin, Pantelic and -- sometime we may change and use another language in order to avoid -- at least we can use both official languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the Bench we are quite satisfied. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: May we have the witness return to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, I would remind the witness that he is still on his oath. Mr. Olmsted, my recollection is that you have completed your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I have about an hour left of it. This is slightly more than we originally planned. The reason being is we spent a lot of time last Thursday going over a lot of little bit dry procedural issues regarding the prosecution service and how cases go through the various procedures. This is important for our case and we think by using this witness to go through those in the future we will be able to cut tremendously on the amount of testimony of other witnesses like this one, but I think we will be finished within the hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First before we begin I would like to make a correction to the record from last Thursday, page 1527, lines 4 and 11 and also page 1531, lines 5 and 9. This is no doubt due to my poor pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, could you spell for us the last name of the basic prosecutor in Sanski Most prior to April 1992, if you could spell his name for us.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sabic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, can you spell that -- spell it out for us?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: S-a-b-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, prior to testifying here today, were you asked to identify -- first of all, when we recessed last Thursday we were -- I was asking you questions about the 1992 KT log-book from your basic prosecutor's office. That was P121. And I'd like to go back to that log-book at this time. We don't need to have it on the screen. Prior to testifying here today you were asked -- were you asked to identify criminal cases listed in this KT log-book in which the perpetrators were Serbs and the victims were non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how many of those cases were you able to identify in the KT log-book?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were seven cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And do you recall -- I suppose you probably off your -- from your memory cannot recall those specific entry numbers?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Is there something that you could refer to that will assist you in recalling the numbers -- the entry numbers of those cases?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were shown a copy of the book, then perhaps I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, as an alternative to that, do you recall making a written statement last week in which you recorded the entry numbers of these seven cases?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, to refresh this witness's recollection, may we show him the written statement that he created last week? We provided this to the Defence and to the Trial Chamber I think it was Wednesday of last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, you've been handed a written statement. Could you please take a look at it and tell us if this is the written statement that you provided last week.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And does this statement refresh your recollection about the number of cases -- actually the entry numbers of the cases in the KT log-book from 1992 in which there was a Serb perpetrator and a non-Serb victim?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: For the record, could you please provide those entry numbers as well as the crimes that the perpetrators were charged with?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first number is KT 110. It was the crime of murder pursuant to Article 36.2 of the Criminal Code of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say there were multiple persons killed. The second number is KT 115. It is the crime of endangering traffic safety, which is Article 181.3. The third case is 120, the crime of rape, Article 88.1. The fourth number is 127, fraud and counterfeiting identification documents. Article 158.2 in relation Article 217.1. The next KT is 129. It says here looting, but it was actually a robbery related to Article 150. Then KT 132, theft in -- from Article 147. Then KT 133, extortion and seizing a motor vehicle, Article 153 and 160.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, for the record the English translation of P121 contains each of these seven entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, so if I understand this correctly, from April to December 1992 the police reported to your office only seven cases in which there was a known Serb perpetrator who committed a crime against a Muslim or a Croat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What does this mean with regard to all of the other numerous crimes that you were describing last Thursday that were occurring against the non-Serb population, all the murders, the grievous bodily injuries, the thefts, the rapes, the destruction of property, what about those cases?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In cases of unidentified perpetrators in the KT log-book, cases were registered as such. The cases were referred to just now involved known perpetrators who had criminal reports submitted against them by the police and were registered as such in the KT log-book that pertains to the cases with identified perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, this means that either the crimes -- all these other crimes that are not here in the KT log-book either went unreported by the police or they were reported by the police as unsolved crimes with unknown perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Which of these seven cases that you listed for us involved a perpetrator who was a member of the police force?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall having any of these cases with a police force perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So would it be accurate to say that no criminal reports against police perpetrators of crimes against non-Serbs were filed with your office in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection. Leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I'll change the questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us from your memory whether any criminal reports against police perpetrators were filed with your office involving crimes against non-Serbs in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall having such a report submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you some questions about two of the entries on the KT log-book, the murder and rape cases which appear to be the only two violent crimes among the seven cases. The first -- the murder case, which is KT entry 110, do you recall this case?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you tell us the facts surrounding this murder, the ethnicity of the victims, the ethnicity of the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The perpetrators were Serbs. One of those reported was Goran Mrdja. In any case, four persons were involved as perpetrators. The victims were two Muslims. The incident took place in the village of Skucani Vakuf. I recall the event, and I attended the scene of crime investigation after the murders took place. Later on a trial was set up to try the perpetrators of the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, under the crimes that the perpetrators were charged, what was the minimum mandatory sentence that they faced?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case we have a qualified murder of several persons. The law envisages the minimum sentence of ten years of imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you mentioned that there was a trial. What sentence was imposed by the basic court in Sanski Most against these perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The perpetrators were sentenced to a term in prison of one year.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, why were they all given only one-year sentences when they should have faced at least ten years?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the lady judge became afraid. In the course of the trial in front of the court building a large group of armed people gathered firing their weapons and they were drunk. A policeman escorting the accused from detention to the court told me that certain individuals from the group wanted to know about me, wanted to know who I was, because I was supposed to present the indictment against those Serbs. They issued threats and the situation was quite tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned that this was an armed group. Could you tell us what the ethnicity of this armed group -- of the members of this armed group was and also what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Serbs since they were complaining about Serbs being tried because they had killed some Muslims. They were in uniform, and they carried long-barrelled weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you know where these armed men in the -- in uniforms -- where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did they fire their weapons that day?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could hear several shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What actions did the police take to prevent these armed men from disrupting the trial?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with any actions the police may have taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And are you aware whether the police ever conducted a criminal investigation into this incident?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would now like to turn to the rape case, which is entry 120 on the KT log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next document is sensitive in nature because it contains not only the victims -- the rape victim's name, but also her location and the facts surrounding the rape. And we ask that it not be published to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we see 65 ter Exhibit 1122. And if we could look at the second page in both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, if you look at the top of page 2, what sentence did the perpetrator of this crime receive for raping a Muslim woman?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were supposed to serve a term in prison of one year, which will not be executed unless the accused commits a new crime within two years. It was a suspended sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Is this an appropriate sentence for a rape case of this nature?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say it was an appropriate sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could look at page 5, paragraph 4, of this document, which is also page 5, paragraph 4 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we can see here that the Court justifies the perpetrator's suspended sentence by providing a number of mitigating factors including, and I'll quote: "That the victim has changed her address as did the majority of locals of the same ethnicity, making it reasonable to expect that mere cautioning combined with the threat of punishment will have sufficient effect on the accused to stop him from committing the same or similar crimes in the future." Mr. Delic, are such considerations appropriate when determining what sentence to impose upon an accused?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such an explanation is probably a result of the circumstances in which the trial took place, that is to say the state of war. I suppose that is why such a mild sentence was pronounced. Perhaps the best person to explain this to you would be the president of the chamber that issued this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, is this another instance where the Court was under pressure or intimidation to impose a low sentence for a crime against a non-Serb?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely, most likely that was the reason for such a mild sentence in relation to a sentence that may have been pronounced in -- under other conditions such as those prevailing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this exhibit be admitted into evidence under seal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P122 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, what measures did the police undertake to protect you and the members from the court from pressure or intimidation when you attempted to prosecute Serbs for crimes against non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any protective measures having been taken then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how interested were the police in ensuring that there were full investigations of these kind of cases where it was a Serb perpetrator and a non-Serb victim?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what to say, but I suppose that they did as much as they could under the circumstances. It is difficult to provide a precise answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, if it was a Serb perpetrator and a Serb victim were the police more willing to fully investigate that case during this time-period, the 1992 time-period?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such cases too where both the perpetrator of the crime and the victim were of the same ethnicity, and the police undertook the same actions from within their remit. There were reports or, rather, I received reports about such cases too.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, we have been discussing -- there was quite a number of crimes against non-Serbs that were never prosecuted in 1992. How did the non-Serb population -- civilian population in Sanski Most react to the failure of the criminal justice system to protect them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The non-Serb population was very frightened at the time. They were mostly trying to leave the territory of the municipality by whichever means. They were extremely scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the non-Serb civilian population's attitude towards the police and the work of the police?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had few contacts with non-Serbs. The neighbours with whom I had contact were simply frightened. The entire situation, the beginning of the war and all that, took us all by surprise. And the very fact that crimes were being committed affected the population in the sense that they were scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did the non-Serb population trust the police?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to answer that question. You would have to ask someone who lived -- someone of non-Serb ethnicity who at the time lived in the territory of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. Let's take a look at 65 ter Exhibit 1788. Now, this is a report by the SJB Sanski Most to CSB Banja Luka, and on the first page it appears to list a number of crimes of violence committed against non-Serbs between the end of October and the beginning of November. First of all, have you -- did you see this document back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at page 2, paragraph 1. In the B/C/S version it's page 2, the second full paragraph. Now, in this paragraph the Sanski Most police chief states, I quote: "At this moment we know who some of the perpetrators are; however, we think that in a situation like this we neither can nor is it advisable to undertake measures of arresting and criminal prosecution because of the safety of SJB employees and legal organs." Mr. Delic, were you aware that at the time you were receiving the significant number of unsolved cases of crimes against non-Serbs that the police were withholding the names of physical perpetrators of these crimes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection. It would be fair for this witness to say - my learned friend said the significant number of unsolved cases. Maybe my colleague can clarify that with the witness, simply asking him: Did you receive a number of criminal charges or complaints against unidentified person. Because it's not clear here in this question, and that will call for speculation of course, that -- it is not the way what this witness explained, a significant number of unsolved cases. Number one, police is not in charge to solve the cases; it is the duty of the prosecution. And he explained that in detail. So maybe you can rephrase your question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. I thought we were going to get another speaking objection there. What I will do is I will just rephrase the question to simplify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, it actually strikes me that a number of questions that you have been -- you have been asking for conclusions, and I'm surprised that this is the first objection that I have heard. So you will rephrase your question accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, were you aware during this time-period, I think this document is from November 1992, that the police were withholding names of physical perpetrators of these crimes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not familiar with that. I saw a mention of a case on page 1, the murder of nine persons of Croatian ethnicity. I know that case. I was there at the on-site investigation, and I know that the perpetrators of that crime were or had been reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, did you ever have a conversation with the police in which you stated you were unwilling to prosecute any of these cases due to your own security concerns?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If the police had brought you one of these cases fully investigated and provided you the names of the perpetrators, would you have refused to prosecute them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was my duty to prosecute persons who had committed crimes and about whom the police had filed criminal reports, and if there was -- there was a foundation for considering these persons really having been the perpetrators of that crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this document be marked for identification purposes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P123, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would now like to turn to the issue of arrests and detention of non-Serbs in Sanski Most during the 1992 time-period --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. Could we try and elicit from Judge Delic if he knows whether or who would put threats or intimidations to policemen if the policemen were to have undertaken these investigations and prosecutions. Who exactly were they afraid of? Was it -- is it possible to identify anyone or any group who would put threats to the policemen if they actually did their job? Would it be the military, or would it be other policemen, or would it be mobs in the Serb community? Or who -- from who did the witness conceive any threats?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, did you understand the question that the Trial Chamber has asked?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you provide us an answer?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that. I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if we could take a look at -- again at P117.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I've just been told it's not been in the system so the 65 ter number is 641. Yeah, that's the correct document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the first paragraph we can see that it's discussing a number of arrests of non-Serbs between May and July of 1992 and their detention at various facilities including the SJB building, sports hall, and Manjaca camp. And while that -- while we take a look at 65 ter Exhibit 10128.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, it's 10.25, according to the clock on the wall -- -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. It's 10.25 according to the clock on the wall. So as I indicated earlier, although we had a late start we would take the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could have 65 ter Exhibit 10128 back on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, this document is dated approximately one month after the one we looked at before, this one, and it's -- it discusses persons detained at the SJB building again in Sanski Most as well as Manjaca camp as well as a factory called Krings. Mr. Delic, were you aware of the existence of these various detention facilities back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What, if any, detention facilities were you aware of that existed in Sanski Most back in 1992 between April and December?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had only heard of the people's front stadium -- sorry, gym. And I heard that the population of the Mahala settlement had been placed there because I met a typist from the court, and I heard that she was placed there for a relatively short period.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was that gym also known as a sports hall?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a sports hall, a gymnasium.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you tell us what were the ethnicities of the people who were held at that facility?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were predominantly persons of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you yourself visit that facility?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How many criminal reports did the police file with your office concerning that detention facility or any other detention facility in Sanski Most during this time-period that was holding non-Serb detainees?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no such criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If you could take a look at the last paragraph of this document in front you, the last sentence it says: "Please inform us on which office of the prosecutor is authorised to deal with this so that we can submit the criminal reports to them." Mr. Delic, why would there be any uncertainty over which prosecutor's office was authorised to accept criminal reports concerning the people held at these various detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly the person who wrote this text was addressing the military prosecution, so possibly the person had in mind acts within the remit of the military prosecution or the court martial.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, can we take a look at P117 again, and if we can look at the end of the first paragraph of this document where it says: "Persons who fled from the place where combat operations were being conducted, about 500 of them who are able-bodied who are being treated as civilian prisoners have been accommodated in the sports hall." Mr. Delic, given that it says here that they're civilians who are being detained there, what would this tell you with regard to which prosecution office they should be filed with if there are any criminal reports concerning these detainees?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the Mahala housing development at Sanski Most, there had been an armed conflict and then the civilian population was removed from that housing development and was put up at the gymnasium where they stayed for a couple of days, after which I know they were taken to another territory somewhere around Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: However, it was assumed that they had committed a crime were they were being held prisoners and they're civilians, which prosecutor's office should the police file that criminal report with, the military or the civilian prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it had been in the remit of the military prosecution, then they would be in charge. For example, if the incriminated act had been armed rebellion because that's within the remit of court martial. In that gymnasium there were many children and women and elderly people who hadn't committed any crime. I suppose they were placed there temporarily because there was armed conflict going on in that housing development where they had been living.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If the police had filed a criminal report with your office and you later determined that it actually belonged within the jurisdiction of the military court, what would you have done?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have submitted such a report to the prosecution into which jurisdiction this falls.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, under the criminal procedure code that was in effect during this time-period, how long could the police detain a person without seeking an order from the Court to extend that person's detention?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think up to three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could we take a look at P120 and page 58 of the English, page 152 of the B/C/S. I'm sorry, I stand corrected. It's page 59 of the English, page 162 of the B/C/S. If you could scroll down. Let's look at Article 196, paragraph number 3. Mr. Delic, if you can please look at that provision, and could you tell us, is this the provision that limits the police to detaining a person for up to three days without a court order?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In paragraph 3 reads: "Pre-trial custody ordered by law enforcement agency may not last longer than three days counted from the hour of deprivation of liberty." That's the provision pertaining to the duration of police detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the detainees that were mentioned in these two documents that we looked at just a moment ago, do you recall the police filing any requests with the Court or with your office seeking to extend their detention beyond three days?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that there were any such requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What categories were non-Serb detainees divided into once they are arrested by the police?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look at Exhibit P60.10. Now, this is a 4 June 1992 Sanski Most Crisis Staff conclusion, and if you can look at the first conclusion, and in particular, the three categories of prisoners. Number 1, the first category politicians; the second category, nationalist extremists; and the third category, people unwelcome in Sanski Most municipality. Mr. Delic, were you aware that the police and the military were dividing non-Serb prisoners into these three categories?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. I had no access to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us under what criminal laws or in fact any laws of the Republika Srpska that the police were authorised to arrest and detain persons for being politicians or because they were unwelcome in the community?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have an objection if you allow. It doesn't follow from the document that the police made this categorisation. The OTP is leading the witness to a wrong conclusion. This is a document by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Olmsted, it seems to me that there's merit in the objection. Again, you're asking a conclusion of the witness from a document which the document doesn't necessarily -- doesn't necessarily support, but more importantly it's a document that he didn't make. So again, can you rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sure, Your Honour. I would just make a note that the conclusion says Mirko Vrucinic who we've established is the chief of police and it says that he is tasked -- he's in charge of resolving the issue of prisoners and categorisation, so that's where the Prosecution had developed that question, but I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, are you aware of any criminal laws or any laws within the Republika Srpska that would permit anyone, be it police, military, whoever, to arrest and detain persons based upon any of these categories, politicians, extremists, people unwelcome in the Sanski Most area?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such law or regulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was remiss. I should have asked for 65 ter Exhibit 10128 to be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I can't remember how far back that was, but I suppose so, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, that was the one we just -- prior to this document that we showed -- or two prior, I'm sorry, it was before the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yeah, it's page 16, line 19.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P124 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that concludes the Prosecution's examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Since I haven't had a chance to wish you a good morning this morning yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My name is Slobodan Cvijetic. I'm a co-counsel in the Defence team of the accused Mico Stanisic. Mr. Delic, in the introductory part of your testimony, that is to say during the examination-in-chief, you said that in your work you basically used three types of law: The penal code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; the Law on Criminal Procedure, which was also enforced at the federal level, and both laws were applied across the SFRY; lastly, you relied on the republican criminal law of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Once I have put my question, please make a short break for the interpreters to be able to interpret since we speak the same language. I am cautioning you although I'm frequently cautioned myself. I would like to take a step back to see how it came about that these laws were being implemented and incorporated into the body of law in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- in Republika Srpska. You will agree that with disintegration of the former SFRY, new states were created in its former territory. You will agree, however, that it was not sufficient to issue a declaration of independence or sovereignty alone. This would not automatically make a state. One of the first issues was to have an entire system or body of law as a single system by implementing what may have amounted to hundreds of new regulations and laws. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree that that kind of work could not be done in 24 hours. There was a looming danger of what I would term a legal void until all regulations are put in place. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Specifically, in your domain that could have presented a great danger because in keeping with the continental legality principle, no one could be prosecuted for crimes committed unless that type of crime as such is envisaged in the existing laws. Does this accurately reflect the principle I outlined?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: If you as a prosecutor at that point in time, you do not have a penal code at your disposal or the Law on Criminal Procedure, you have nothing to work with. It's not only you but also the investigating judge and the police who couldn't undertake measures to prosecute perpetrators of crime. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That is why all of the former republics, including Republika Srpska, came up with a model of filling in that legal void by putting into force separate regulations with immediate effect following a special procedure by which it was determined that until new regulations are in place the old regulations were to be applied, that is to say the regulations of the former SFRY and the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you know of that procedure?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would kindly ask for 1D00-4266 to be shown to the witness. Let me see what this page is. Could we scroll up in the B/C/S. Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, on the left-hand side in the bottom right corner - and I think you need to scroll up in the English as well so that the Chamber may follow - it is the decision on the implementation of the constitutional law -- for the implementation of the constitution of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you recall this particular regulation, the decision to implement the constitution of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now you can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, now let's go to the next page, in particular Article 12 of the law. The next page, please. There. Please do the same in the English. Article 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Delic, read out this article --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Article 12 it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You can read it for yourself. Are you familiar with this particular provision?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to read it at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was the legal basis for the implementation of the former regulations of the SFRY and the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which did not contravene the regulations put into force by Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the document I seek to tender it as a Defence exhibit since my colleague, the Prosecutor, was able to identify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Hadn't it been decided that all laws -- I suppose whichever side relied on it would be put into one basket, rather than having them exhibited individually? Even if they had to be somehow internally identified by somehow -- but they did have to be exhibited by other documentary exhibits. Wouldn't this fall into the category?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it will be so; however, in expectation of the realisation of that agreement, time is passing by, and we frequently refer to certain laws. I believe it was on the Prosecution's proposal. You already admitted certain regulations. It will be as you say, but I'm now dealing with a rather short law which was easy to comment upon. I agree with the system you put forth, but at this point in time I need to have this law commented upon by the witness and made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I understand what you are in the process of doing. It's merely the matter of the -- there being no necessity to have it marked as an exhibit. It's just put into the -- whatever mechanism is in use for adding to this basket of laws would be followed in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I accept your suggestion. I would kindly ask that this agreement between the OTP and us be implemented as soon as possible. We are constantly being told that it will be so, but it did not see the light of day yet. In any case, I agree with your proposal, and I believe we had the witness sufficiently comment upon the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, Article 12 was the basis of introducing certain criminal regulations and provisions into the body of law of Republika Srpska, and you will agree with me that in the body of law in Republika Srpska that was being used at the time there may have been dozens or even hundreds of regulations of the former SFRY and the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I cannot guarantee, but I think there are still individual regulations in force from that period that are still used. You are now a notary and you are duty-bound to implement these laws, and this particular law was only removed about a year ago?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that. We had the new law on the application that was put into force on the 5th of January this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Therefore, we dealt with the issue of the introduction of these regulations into the body of law. I would now like to dwell upon the manner in which you were elected prosecutor. Before that, since we have already been discussing provisions of the criminal law, I would like to go over a few questions put to you by the Prosecutor. Namely, the Criminal Code of the SFRY is split into two parts; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It had its general part containing the legal principles and a separate part in which there were types of crimes specified which were of federal level. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In that separate part there were such crimes as those directed against the basis of the socialist state system, then crimes against humanity and international law. It was only the SFRY who figured as the signatory of the various international conventions, and it was under an obligation to include the laws pertaining to such conventions into its domestic law, that is to say in the most general sense the crimes pertaining to the situations of war or war crimes in general. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Then these offences included also crimes directed against the armed forces, where I can particularly stress the crimes of espionage, sabotage, and armed rebellion. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What is particularly interesting in this chapter is the fact that civilians could be held criminally responsible if found to have committed such crimes. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In peacetime, you will agree, there were military courts which processed such cases. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This would be it concerning the criminal code, and I would like to move on to the Law on Criminal Procedure. Mr. Delic, a criminal procedure begins, so to say, in the court building by the -- by virtue of a decision issued by an investigating judge on the opening of an investigation or by raising an indictment or a proposal for indictment issued by the public prosecutor. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Therefore, an investigation is initiated, conducted, and concluded by the investigating judge; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I won't go into all the different provisions of the Law on Criminal Procedure since we are both professionals, and I suppose you will not dispute anything regarding this part. I used to be a prosecutor myself some 30 years ago and I still recall these provisions. The police does not conduct a criminal procedure and does not carry out an investigation; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that the police merely initiates a criminal procedure which, as you said yourself, happened in some 90 per cent of the cases. However, a criminal procedure can also be initiated by any other entity, and in your view there was some 10 per cent of such cases. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In Article 162 of that law it says that an investigating judge can only entrust some investigative actions to a body of the interior - we will use the term police - and then the police has to carry out that order in keeping with the order of the investigating judge. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let us say an investigating judge orders a -- an apartment to be searched, and he himself is not in a position to attend that search himself, in that case he can order the police to carry out the search and to report back to him. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, criminal proceedings are finalised when the investigation is dropped, for example, if you as a prosecutor give up on further criminal procedure; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Or in passing a judgement in which the trial chamber or a judge will decide on the lot of the criminal proceedings; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You can also reject criminal charges and you don't have to initiate criminal proceedings; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In that case you will agree with me that the police does not decide, they don't decide either on the start, the course, or the finalisation of criminal procedure. Everything is within the purview of the organs of the judiciary. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And now I'm coming to the issue of your appointment that I've already announced. You have already told us about the democratic procedure by way of which you were elected. It seems that you were given an offer that you couldn't refuse; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You still owe us an answer as to what would have been a regular procedure for the election of a judge or a prosecutor. Who would have been in charge of electing those people?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Previously it was the Assembly or, rather, the Assemblies.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce Exhibit 65 ter -- from 65 ter list 713.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, before we see the document let me just ask you this: Did you know your colleague, your fellow prosecutor from Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His name was Aleksa Tepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Aleksa Tepic, very well then. Could you please look at the left-hand side of your screen which should display the B/C/S version of the document. Could you look at paragraph 2. Look at the first bullet point. I believe that the B/C/S version should be moved slightly to the right. The English version is okay, but could you please move the B/C/S version slightly to the right. And now you can see the first bullet point under paragraph 2. Could you please look at it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read it to you if you can't read - I believe you can - however, let me read it for you. "Momcilo and Cedo are to settle together with Goran the matter of the public prosecutor ..." Could you please look at the title of the document and see who the issuer of the document was. This is an excerpt of the -- from the minutes of the session of the Crisis Staff of Kotor Varos. And here the Crisis Staff decides to settle the matter of the public prosecutor in Kotor Varos. It seems that this choice or this election, rather, is even more out of the ordinary than was yours. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution objects to this line of questioning. The Defence is asking the witness to comment on occurrences in another municipality separate from his own, and I don't think there's enough foundation for him to be answering these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- Mr. Olmsted, as I understand the Prosecution's purpose in tendering this witness, it was -- he spoke largely from the questions that were put by the Prosecution in terms of systems and methods that were in place; and against that background I am not sure I see where the Defence is off base. Because, again although they talk about a different municipality, the question as I understand it goes to the structures and systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, well our line of questioning regarding this witness's -- the personnel changes within his municipality were based upon his factual knowledge of what happened in that municipality. He did -- was not giving evidence on generally the hiring and firing of prosecutor witnesses -- or prosecutors or judges during this time-period. And now the Defence is asking him questions about an entirely different municipality, to which he -- there's no foundation that he actually had contact with those people over there. So he's basically asking him to give an opinion based upon procedures in a different municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And if I may, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I please --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And this witness just mentioned his colleague from Kotor Varos, Mr. Aleksa Tepic, who was a public prosecutor in Kotor Varos. That's a link, that's enough link because he just mentioned that he knew prosecutor from Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. I'm not sure, myself, that that's sufficient of a link. But, Mr. Cvijetic, we're assuming that you had laid a foundation for what you're asking, where are you headed? What do you seek to elicit by this line of questioning? And I understand -- I take Mr. Olmsted's point about a foundation having to be laid by you in order to ask the question you're about to ask because you're dealing with -- you've moved to matters outside of the personal experience of this witness, even if he is talking about systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in commenting my questions you have rightly guessed my intention when you just responded to the Prosecutor. I don't intend to have that document admitted. I am just talking about the context that the Prosecutor -- that the witness is talking about and has already discussed with the Prosecutor. I'm talking about very strange ways of electing public prosecutors. Here they're elected by the Crisis Staff. I'm not going to have this document admitted. He knew the fellow prosecutor, and he can also tell us that his election was quite odd and so was the election of his fellow prosecutor in Kotor Varos. I'm just trying to put things in to a certain context. And when it comes to municipalities I'm already on the way back to the municipality where the gentleman served as a prosecutor, and in that sense I have already laid the foundation when I asked him how he was elected. And the Prosecutor asked him the same thing, and this is my foundation for the questions that I'm going to be putting to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And sorry to interrupt, just for the record, Mr. Tully just informed me that this particular document was exhibit -- admitted as Exhibit P85. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, let's go back to the municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown 1D00-4513. That's the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, please look at the document. Again, the left-hand side of the screen. And could you please pay attention to bullet point 2 or item 2. This is another document issued by the Crisis Staff, and in this particular case it was the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Sanski Most where you worked and resided. Crisis Staff issues orders to a number of different entities. You can see which entities those were and we are interested in bullet point 2 where it says: "The president of the Sanski Most lower court is ordered to provide a forensic judge for the burial of the dead." I'm still talking about the context. Here the Crisis Staff issued an order to the president of the lower court and ordered him as to what and how to work. Mr. Delic, did you know anything about this way of work of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Sanski Most? Did they meddle with the work of the judiciary bodies?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can speak for myself. They didn't meddle with my work, and I've not seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In any case, you have just been shown what they dealt with. I'm not going to insist on the admittance of this document because you are not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have a document from 65 ter list. The number is 606. We're interested in bullet point 2 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, could you please read bullet point 2 for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Go on then. Will you agree with me that it says here that the Crisis Staff appoints and certifies that Mirko Vrucinic shall begin to work as the acting chief of the public security station of Sanski Most and that he will be issued a decision to that effect? I'm not going to ask you about the document. It's self-explanatory. Given the fact that you were a prosecutor at the time, are you in the least familiar with the structure and hierarchy in the MUP? That's my first question. In principle, you don't have to be familiar with all the details.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And this kind or this procedure to elect Mr. Mirko Vrucinic, was it in compliance with the way the highest officials in the Ministry of the Interior should have been appointed as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was not a customary way to appoint officials in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: How should this have been done?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, there should have been a procedure in place and it should have been followed for the election of the chief of a public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Delic, let's leave all the documents aside for the time being. I have more of them but let's take a break from the documents. I would like to talk to you about the conditions of your work in Sanski Most. You've already spoken about that in answering the Prosecutor's questions, but let me put some very concrete questions to you in this regard. In the initial stages of your work, did you suffer from a communication breakdown? Was there enough electricity or were there frequent outages? And was your movement restricted; and if it was, to what extent? I've asked several questions - I apologise - but I believe that they're all related. Could you please answer.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of May and in early June 1992, the entire Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina saw the outbreak of conflicts. In Sanski Most there were also armed conflicts. To put it simply, there was no electricity for over two months. During that summer all sorts of communication lines, for example, telephone lines were down most of the time. And it was really very difficult to establish communication with Banja Luka or any other towns. In the area the movement of people was restricted. You could not leave town. There were frequent controls at check-points, and at those check-points there were armed members of the army. You could not move without a pass. As far as the supply of staple foods are concerned, there was no food to be had. Stores were empty. Their shop windows were broken. The situation was very chaotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe you have painted a very good picture of the situation. You will agree with me that at that time there was that big operation to break through the corridor. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: After the breakthrough through the corridor, was it safe to use that military road?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not safe in the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and my municipality was no exception to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But let's focus on the corridor. Was it a target of constant attacks, bombing, even after it was officially opened?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all sorts of incidents took place there quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And let's now talk about the organisation of the work of the prosecutor. When did you learn who your republican public prosecutor was?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember, but it was later on, at a later stage. Maybe as late as 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you will allow for the possibility that it was perhaps even after the war in 1995 or even 1996 that you learned who your public prosecutor was?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, it does not seem very usual that -- can you briefly explain how this occurred?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The office of the prosecutor was in Pale and Pale was far then. It is still far, and it was especially far during the war given the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So let's just say that Pale is in the eastern part of Republika Srpska across from the corridor. Would I be right in putting it that way?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And what about the higher public prosecutor, senior public prosecutor, where was his office?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His office was in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: When did you first meet to the public prosecutor who was superior to you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than two months elapsed or must have elapsed when I was appointed public prosecutor at Sanski Most and when I met the senior public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Good. At Pale there was the headquarters of the most important public authorities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go to Pale during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, when did you find out who the minister of the interior was and what his name was at that period?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe after the war when newspapers started to write about that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This case or the case of Jovica Stanisic and that's when you made the link?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a while there was -- there were many reports about Jovica Stanisic. I suppose that Mico and Jovica are related based on their last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: No, actually they aren't, but they do have the same last name. So we will agree that only when these proceedings started before the Tribunal you found out who the minister of the interior was in 1992; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, and when you were replying to the questions of the Prosecutor you said that it can be best seen from the log-book how there was a -- how it happened that there was a surge of crime in the territory of the Sanski Most municipality. You said that from the log-book for 1991 reaching till May 1992, it can clearly be seen that most violations committed were petty offences. You even meant theft of wood in the forest, et cetera. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And then you said that as of May 1992 one could witness a drastic difference; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: At once you were faced with the most dangerous sort of crime in your territory. There were murders, robberies, et cetera. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me when I say that was a novelty which burdened both law enforcement, that is the police, and you as a prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I will try to elaborate on the example of Sanski Most with you. All police forces in the world have an operational register. Do you know of that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In that register they internally, for their own purposes, register persons who are suspected of engaging in criminal activity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: However, the -- that is based only on assumptions so there is not enough to establish so-called founded suspicion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So the police keeps track of them until there is founded evidence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: For Sanski Most I believe that you can't give us the exact numbers but you can give us a description, what the situation was in that aspect and how many persons there were in that register as potential perpetrators of crimes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have available the statistics, but since Sanski Most was a small place and a quiet place, where before the war crimes were rare and the crimes committed were not so dangerous for the entire society. I suppose that in the so-called operational register of the police there were persons who engaged in such activity which was not so very dangerous for the society.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. But then you were aware of the enormous rise in crime. Can one word, which I'm about to say, outline the reasons for that event, and that word is war? Is that the word that can best explain what started happening then?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When war broke out the most serious crimes started being committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So when the war started, war-time activities, in the territory of Sanski Most, there was the arrival of military formations. But you will agree with me parallelly to them and independently who also arrived were paramilitary formations, criminals who had put on uniforms and who had weapons, in other words, persons who were not to be found in the operational register of the police because they had come from elsewhere and they were constantly on the move. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably but my movement was restricted so that I do not have much information about the movement of these persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just a foundational objection here. I think the witness established that he agreed that there was a -- some kind of operational register of the police. But now the line of questioning is with regard to what was in that register. And I don't think it's been established whether this witness ever saw that register or ever took a look at what was written in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In any event, the witness said he couldn't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Before I move on to the next question, I will try to define the times that you have depicted by quoting a famous sentence of our only Nobel literature prize winner from the region, and I will ask you know that sentence. "There comes a time when fools speak, intelligent people are quiet, and ragtag and bobtail gets rich." Does that sentence describe those times?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that sentence. It was written by Ivo Andric, the Nobel literature prize winner, and it depicts wartime very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, we will now speak about your KTN log-book about which the OTP has already asked you. Do you know what a black spot in crime means?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that should refer to the number of undiscovered perpetrators of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Correct. That is the ratio of the crimes committed to crimes resolved. You will agree with me that that black spot, that is the number of unresolved crimes, in regular, normal times when the judiciary bodies and the police functioned well should be smaller; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But at the times you also lived through, you will agree with me, also had to contribute to the fact that that black spot was greater?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: By submitting a criminal report against an unknown perpetrator, or rather, that -- such a submission is based on the law; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The criminal procedures act in Article 151 says that the police, apart from identifying the perpetrator, urgently must secure evidence about -- of the commission of the -- or the commitment of the crime. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Line -- page 42, line 5, between 5 and 8, our friend from interpreter's booth did not correctly translated what witness said. Witness said that police should secure crime scene, crime scene. So let's clarify that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, just once again thanks for your intervention, but please do not try and put into the mouths of the witnesses what you think they said. It's better to have it directly from themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, in any case, Mr. Pantelic, whether you heard it or not is irrelevant. So the important thing is that we get it directly from the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- and not from counsel. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, let us then clarify this part. It is the task of the police, among other things, to secure and keep evidence that remains after a crime has been committed. Did we speak about that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the evidence found on the crime scene must be found and preserved. That should be the sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I understood you also, and that's also what the law says. Speaking about which, let me say that there is a saying in the police that at such moments it is more important to secure evidence than run after the perpetrator, because what good is it if you cannot indict him later on and there is no foundation for the court to convict him. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. We're done with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It has been suggested to me that we should clarify that this is the very purpose of submitting a criminal report against an unknown perpetrator; namely, to secure all evidence in a legal manner in order to be able to use them once a perpetrator is found. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let's say biological traces and evidence will perish, and unless they are collected and secured they can never be renewed again. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us not go into that any further. I believe we have clarified sufficiently. I would like to go into some new circumstances that changed the situation in your municipality. Parallelly to the functioning of the civilian judiciary authorities and bodies, court's martial, military prosecutors, and military police come to the scene; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like an exhibit from the 65 ter list to be put to the witness. It is marked number 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, on the right-hand side of this document, as you see, there is a decision on the establishment seat and jurisdiction of military courts and military prosecutor's offices. And -- on the right-hand side, yes, right here, just this. Can you see it? And if I'm not mistaken, let us take a look. So military courts and military prosecutor's offices are established and by -- under this decision they are linked to the corps commands. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what follows from this decision.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat. You are going too fast for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, the interpreters are asking that you slow down the pace.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the part on the top. When does this decision come into force? In the upper left-hand side corner. Do you see the date?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 31st of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But it comes into force eight days after publication, and it was published on the 31st of May; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Simultaneously with the regular courts, the military courts were being established. I don't know whether you were familiar with this, but I have with me a decision on the election, jurisdiction, and establishment of courts of the Autonomous Region of Krajina which followed the establishment of military courts. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Then I won't ask you about this, but I hope you will take my word for it that first military courts were formed and then civilian courts. Since we have had a look at this document, next I would kindly ask for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, it's -- before you move on to your next question, it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay, okay. [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
